risks: Hydrogen economics and capital intensity remain major execution constraints despite improving unit/service economics.
Break-even gross margin is a milestone, not yet proof of durable consolidated profitability or self-funding operations.
Vertical integration improves control but concentrates execution burden across manufacturing, hydrogen production, logistics and end-use equipment.
Battery-electric substitutes can erode hydrogen's advantage in duty cycles where charging downtime and infrastructure are manageable.
Continued operating cash consumption leaves financing/dilution sensitivity material until operations become durably self-funding.
A vertically integrated network can amplify fixed-cost and utilization risk if hydrogen demand or plant ramp trails expectations.
Customer refresh intentions and backlog-like demand signals should not be equated with realized revenue until conversion occurs.
unknowns: Customer refresh plans are prospective and conversion timing is not assured.
Path and timing to durable positive free cash flow remain unproven.
Long-run utilization and delivered hydrogen cost across the planned DOE-supported network are not yet demonstrated at mature scale.
Future external financing mix and resulting dilution cannot be established from current evidence.
Mature economics of each planned hydrogen facility remain unproven.
contradictions: Operational and margin improvement coexists with continued net cash consumption.
Greater vertical integration can improve supply reliability while simultaneously increasing capital intensity and financing dependence.
Break-even gross margin and improving service economics coexist with substantial consolidated net losses and operating cash use.
